bio.en: Archie Abrams is VP of Product and Head of Growth at Shopify, leading a 600+ person org (product, design, engineering, data ops, growth marketing) and formerly a long-time leader at Udemy; he turned Shopify's "build a 100-year company" long-termism, its long-horizon holdout experiments, and its use of absolute numbers over conversion rates into an operational growth practice.
bio.zh: Archie Abrams 是 Shopify 的产品 VP 兼增长负责人，领导一个 600 多人的组织（产品、设计、工程、数据运营、增长营销），曾长期任职于 Udemy；他把 Shopify「为 100 年建公司」的长期主义、用长期 holdout 实验衡量真实影响、以及用绝对数而非转化率做增长指标的方法，变成了可执行的增长实践。

summary.en: Archie Abrams shares Shopify's counterintuitive growth philosophy: because revenue comes mostly from payments tied to merchant success (not subscriptions), they don't optimize for retention/churn but lower the barrier to starting a business and let a few huge winners (a power law) carry each cohort's value. They keep 1–3 year holdouts on every experiment and found ~30–40% of short-term "wins" have no long-term lift (mostly pull-forward effects) — so teams still ship short-term wins and even "neutral" experiments. On metrics, Shopify uses absolute counts, not conversion rates, to stop teams from tightening the upstream funnel just to flatter their local rate. The org splits into core product (decided by Tobi/Glen on taste, no KPIs), growth R&D, growth marketing, and customer support; growth and core collaborate through healthy tension and trust. He also covers the attribution mess of blending sales and self-serve funnels, Shopify's CMO-less embedded marketing, and how Udemy used discounts to signal value through price and trigger an emotional sense of progress.
summary.zh: Archie Abrams 分享了 Shopify 反直觉的增长哲学：因为收入主要来自商家成功后的支付分成（而非订阅），所以他们不优化「留存/流失」，而是降低创业门槛、让更多商家进门，靠少数大成商家（幂律）撑起整批价值。他们为跑过的每个实验保留 1–3 年的长期 holdout，发现约 30–40% 短期显示 lift 的实验长期其实没增量（多为「提前拉动」效应）——所以团队仍会 ship 短期有效的改动，甚至 ship「中性」实验。指标上，Shopify 用绝对人数而非转化率，避免团队为美化局部转化率而收紧上游漏斗。组织上分核心产品（由 Tobi/Glen 凭品味决策、无 KPI）、增长 R&D、增长营销、客户支持；增长与核心靠「健康张力」和信任协作。他还聊了销售+自助混合漏斗的归因难题、无 CMO 的嵌入式营销，以及 Udemy 用折扣「用价格 signal 价值+触发情感进步」的打法。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: When you have teams naturally break up the world into different funnel stages or different points in the journey, it gets very seductive to look at my part of the funnel and what's my conversion rate through that part of the funnel, right? And then the team starts to optimize for that conversion rate as their north star. But in practice, it's actually almost always easier to just make it harder to do the thing right before your step in the funnel to increase your conversion rate. Instead of I'm trying to convert a bunch of people, I just want more people to get activated. (00:00:32): And then once you start thinking that way, you realize actually the best way to get more people to get to a step is just get more people in the door in the first place. That will always hurt your conversion rate, but it may actually give you more people on the outside.
turns.zh: 当团队自然地把世界拆成不同的漏斗阶段或旅程的不同节点时，会非常有诱惑去看「我这部分漏斗、我这段的转化率是多少」，对吧？然后团队就开始把那个转化率当成他们的北极星来优化。但实际上，几乎总是更容易的做法是：让你漏斗里你这步之前的那步更难做，从而抬高你的转化率。所以与其我想转化一堆人，我更想要更多人被激活 (activated)。一旦你开始那么想，你会意识到，其实让更多人到达某步的最好方式，往往就是一开始就让更多人进门。那永远会伤害你的转化率，但它可能真的给你更多在门外的人。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: The way we think about churn is really going back to Shopify as a kind of our mission and what we want to do, which is to increase the amount of entrepreneurship on the internet. And so as a business, we want to make it as easy as possible to get started with your online store, with your business. (00:07:06): But most businesses do ultimately fail. Some of those people on their first attempt that's entrepreneurship might not succeed, but the folks who do go on to be successful will make that entire cohort of merchants who started something that makes Shopify as a business extremely successful. turns.zh: 我们想 churn 的方式，真的回到 Shopify 作为使命、我们想做的事——增加互联网上的创业数量。所以作为生意，我们想让开网店、开业务尽可能容易。但大多数生意最终会失败。所以我们看的是：我们能不能降低开始的门槛、让尽可能多的人进门试试创业？如果那么做，很多那些生意、那些人第一次尝试可能不成功，但我们会有一批商家后来变成超大业务——像 Allbirds、FIGS 之类的。Shopify 的商业模式是我们收订阅费，但我们大部分收入来自支付，直接跟商家的成功挂钩。所以在一批商家 (cohort) 里，很多人会开始。有些第一次试创业可能不成功，但那些真成功的，会让整批开始的商家让 Shopify 作为生意极其成功。那就是我们为什么降低开始的门槛、帮人们成长，而那些赢家让整件事转起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny

And all you need is a few big wins for it to all work out.

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams

turns.zh: 对。那跟大多数 SaaS 公司真不同——他们拿到一个客户，就绝不想那人离开。而我们想降低开始的门槛、让人成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny

I imagine there's almost an implied it's really cheap for you all to find new customers because of maybe the brand and word of mouth. Is that true?

(00:10:56): Again, going back to investing, same thing there. Each vintage from a fund, how much did that return as a fund? And it's really driven by the few really successful outliers.
turns.zh: 这种方式是看我们在某时间段（比如一季）获取的这批用户。然后在接下来的一、二、三、四、五年，那些商家总共产了多少 GMV？不是按商家个体，而是总共，那批商家有没有产 GMV？如果他们产了 GMV，那会转成收入、毛利、以及我们能用来再投资增长业务的所有东西。所以它真看总价值，但是在 GMV 基础上。而 GMV 是个幂律 (power law) 指标。所以是那个幂律驱动每批的成功。回到投资，同理。一个基金每批 (vintage)，作为基金它回报了多少？真由那几个极成功的 outlier 驱动。

And that'll actually change what we do from that previous experiment. And so there's a lot of longterm monitoring of experiments over these very long time horizons to both inform what those input metrics are and more importantly hold ourselves accountable to, did we actually move what we cared about, which is that longterm GMV, in the right way?
turns.zh: 对。好玩的是，Shopify 我们非常刻意地把组织的不同部分设成用非常不同的时间视野、非常不同的方式去思考怎么建产品。跟很多公司很不同——那些公司通常有一个统一的、全公司 rally around 的北极星。Shopify 有三个主要产品组。核心产品 (core product) 基本在建「100 年后的商务该有的正确东西」。商家服务 (merchant services) 建支付、物流、创业者成功需要的工具，视野更短或中期。增长 (growth) 真在想那个端到端的客户旅程——我们怎么带人进来、确保他们成功？从指标角度，增长里我们显然有些领先指标在看某个实验。但我们在实验里想 instrumentation 的关键是看实验长期效果的能力。所以我们会不断在一年后重看一个实验，看那批的 GMV 曲线分布跟我们原来想的不同，那 actually 会改变我们之前那个实验做的。所以有大量在这些很长视野上的长期监控，既为了告知那些输入指标是啥，更重要的是让我们对自己负责——我们真把我们在乎的、那个长期 GMV，朝对的方向推动了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. I want to spend more time here. So the way you're describing it is the way the business operates is you think, what is our 100-year plan? How do we think, where does this need to be in 100 years? And with that, it allows you to run these long holdout experiments to see, is something we're doing impacting the business broadly? And because you think so longterm, you can take a year, or two, or three to see if there's an impact and then make adjustments versus I'm having to drive a certain metric every quarter, every year.
turns.zh: 哇。好，我想在这多待会。你描述的方式是，业务运作是你想「我们的 100 年计划是啥？100 年后这得在哪？」有了那个，它让你跑这些长期 holdout 实验看某事是否 broad 影响业务。因为你这么长期，你能花一、二、三年来看有没有影响、然后调整，而不是我得每季每年驱动某指标。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct. And I mean on growth, we're definitely in the... We want to drive metrics on a short-term basis and we can do that obviously, but we have the luxury, and the way Tobi thinks about the world and the way we operate, to really think about these longterm effects and make sure that we're holding ourselves accountable with these longterm holdouts, and then constantly refining the input metrics that we're using and getting a lot smarter about that. But because we take that long horizon, it allows us to be better in the short term and just get a lot smarter. (00:14:17): And a lot of counterintuitive things. And I would encourage everyone, if you can, look at some of the experiments that you thought were your biggest winners. Look at the downstream metrics for a year, two years on that experiment. And I'll bet you'd be surprised how many times the metric is different than what you thought it would be after a year.
turns.zh: 对。我的意思是增长上我们 definitely 在短期驱动指标、我们 obviously 能做到，但我们有那种奢侈——Tobi 看世界的方式、我们运作的方式——去真想这些长期效果、确保我们用这些长期 holdout 对自己负责，然后不断精炼我们用的输入指标、变得更聪明。但因为我们用长视野，它让我们短期更好、更聪明。很多反直觉的事。我鼓励每个人，如果可以，去看你以为最大赢家的几个实验。看那实验一、两年后的下游指标。我打赌你会惊讶多少次那指标跟你以为的不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because where people just make a call at a certain point in time, here's the list in it, here's the list experience. I love this, because very few people have experiences running a longterm experiment, and so this is a really interesting insight that you're sharing that, I guess how often do you find this to be true in your long-term holdouts, where things end up being very different downstream?
turns.zh: 因为人们只在某个时间点做个判断，这里是列表、这里是列表体验。我爱这个，因为很少有人有跑长期实验的经验，所以你分享的这个洞察真有意思——在你的长期 holdout 里，你多常发现下游非常不同？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: I think there's probably two things that have been very common. And I would say in quite a few cases, you get a lift on a metric up front, a more short-term metric. Number of people who become a paying shopper, number of people who make their first sale in Shopify. And then you look a year later, and there's actually no incremental lift on GMV from that cohort. (00:15:21): And so I think it actually trains, a lot of us in growth are looking at these short-term metrics. A lot of the time it's actually more pull-forward effect, than you fully realize or an incremental user that's just really not worth that much. So that's one. (00:15:35): And then two, so this effect size goes away. There are cases where the experiment has flipped the other way. And then there are cases, and these are the most interesting ones, where you realize that you uncovered a pocket of merchants that are actually extremely valuable entrepreneurs who go on to be successful, that you missed in your normal short-term measurement techniques. And so all across the board we see that. But actually the most common is it actually isn't a long-term lift from a lot of things that you might think of the short-term are.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两件很常见。我会说不少情况下，你 upfront 拿到一个指标的 lift、更短期的指标——变成付费店主的人数、在 Shopify 出第一单的人数。然后你看一年后，那批其实没有增量的 GMV lift。所以我觉得它其实训练了我们增长里很多人看这些短期指标。很多时候它其实是「提前拉动」(pull-forward) 效应，比你 fully 意识到的，或一个真不值那么多的增量用户。那是一。然后二，效应大小消失了。有些 case 实验翻到另一边。还有 case——这些最有趣——你意识到你揭开了一群商家，是真正极有价值的创业者、后来成功了，而你在正常短期测量技术里漏了他们。所以我们到处看到那个。但最常的是，很多你以为短期是 lift 的东西，其实没有长期 lift。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example in that second bucket of what you mean when you say there's a pocket of valuable merchants?
turns.zh: 第二个桶里，你说「一群有价值的商家」，有例子吗？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, I think a lot of this has to do with, we call it monetary friction. So one of the hardest things to do with a business is when you're getting started, is you might not have any revenue coming in, and you are kind of bootstrapping, which in Shopify's case might be 39 bucks a month. But still, it's a real expense. (00:16:43): And so typically when you can lower the barriers to monetary friction in some form, that could be all sorts of monetary friction early. The common belief is that we'll usually get lower quality folks coming in the door, because usually discounts are associated with lower quality. (00:17:03): If you think about in a business case, if I give you a little monetary boost and reduce that monetary friction, I can actually causally change your ability to become successful, because I've given you a little bit more time to try that idea a little bit longer. I've given you that opportunity to move your business over to Shopify. And so often in those types of experiments you see that you've basically unlocked a class of people who might've given up without reducing that monetary friction
turns.zh: 对，我觉得很多跟我们叫「货币摩擦」(monetary friction) 的有关。做生意最难的事之一是一开始你可能没有任何收入进账，你在 bootstrapping——在 Shopify 的情况可能是每月 39 块。但仍是真开销。通常当你能以某种形式降低货币摩擦的门槛——可能是早期各种货币摩擦。常见的信念是我们通常会引来更低质量的进门的人，因为折扣通常跟低质量关联。但如果从商业 case 想，如果我给你一点货币 boost、降低那货币摩擦，我能因果地改变你成功的能力，因为我给了你多一点时间试那点子久一点。我给了你机会把业务搬到 Shopify。所以常在这类实验里你看到你 basically 解锁了一类人——没有降低那货币摩擦他们可能就放弃了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. And giving them time to actually make it work.
turns.zh: 有意思。给他们时间去真让它 work。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: To make it work.
turns.zh: 去让它 work。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So just roughly, do you have a sense of how often you find no effect after a year that you saw early impact? Just to ballpark that.
turns.zh: 好。大致上，你有感觉多久后发现一年后没效果、但早期看到影响？就大致估一下。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, it's in the 30 to 40% range.
turns.zh: 对，大概 30% 到 40% 的范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I think you're tearing the heart out of so many growth people right now, and nobody wants to hear this that works on growth where you're saying potentially a third of the experiments they're running today that are showing lift probably don't have that same... Don't have any impact down the road.
turns.zh: 好。我觉得你在撕很多增长人的心，没人想听这个——你说可能三分之一你们今天跑的、显示 lift 的实验，大概没同样的……没下游影响。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yes. Unfortunately, I think that's brutal. Probably more common than we like to believe.
turns.zh: 对。不幸，我觉得那 brutal。可能比我们愿信的更常见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, and nobody wants to hear this, except people that you should want to hear this because if you want to build a business that grows and need to grow, it's better to know to learn that now.
turns.zh: 对，没人想听这个，除了那些你该想听的人——因为如果你想建个要增长、需要增长的生意，现在知道、学到这个更好。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So for people that can't run whole long hold that experiments, I guess is there anything that you find is a good early indicator that might be the case? Most people don't have time to sit around and wait a year or two or three. They're not thinking 100 years.
turns.zh: 好。对不能跑整个长期 holdout 实验的人，我猜有没有什么好的早期指标能预示这种情况？大多数没时间坐着等一两年三年。他们不想 100 年。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: I mean I think end of the day that is going to be the most effective and you actually learn the most. I think it is, though even in shorter term horizons, really being as specific as you can be about what are the early signs of success in your product, and making sure you instrument those. And then making sure, particularly up funnel experiments, you are actually looking at the further downstream metrics to make sure you have some understanding of what's moving down. (00:19:17): So as deep as you can go in the funnel for as long as you can wait. Do that. And if you can't, you know what I would say? Still you should just bet on, if something is showing lift up funnel, still ship it and it's probably not going to hurt you, but don't overestimate the amount of impact that this is having. (00:19:34): So it's funny, two things here is, my recommendation to folks is don't think, "Oh my goodness, I have to wait all this time." Because if you didn't move the short-term impact, you're not going to have the long-term lift. So still ship if it's short-term lift. Just be reasonable that if you can measure it longer term, you'll get better about identifying what things are that are really impactful.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，归根结底那是最有效、你也学到最多的。但即便在更短视野，真尽可能具体地说出你产品里成功的早期信号是啥、确保你 instrumentation 那些。然后确保——尤其上游实验——你真在看更下游的指标，确保你理解什么在下游动。所以你能在漏斗里钻多深、等多久就钻多深、等多久。做那个。如果你不能，你知道我会说啥？还是应该押注：如果某事上游显示 lift，还是 ship 它，它可能不伤你，但别高估这影响有多大。所以好玩的是两点：我对人们的建议是别想「哦天我得等所有这些时间」，因为如果你没动短期影响，你不会有长期 lift。所以如果短期有 lift 还是 ship。只是理性点：如果你能更长期测，你会更擅长识别啥东西真有影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And so it may be positive initially, but often neutral. Rarely is it neutral initially and then positive down the road?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以可能 initial 正、但常中性。很少是 initial 中性然后下游正？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: There are some cases of that, but it's rarely... I've seen neutral be positive, but I haven't seen negative.
turns.zh: 有那样的情况，但很少……我见过中性变正，但我没见过负变正。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay-
turns.zh: 明白了。好——

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: That resulted positive.
turns.zh: 结果正。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. So that's reassuring. You're not harming the business, but you're probably getting a lot more credit than you deserve as a growth team shipping things that are-
turns.zh: 明白了。好。那挺安慰。你没伤害业务，但作为增长团队 ship 那些东西，你大概得到的 credit 比你该得的更多——

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Likely.
turns.zh: 可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Likely, right?
turns.zh: 可能，对吧？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Likely.
turns.zh: 可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's also just trade-offs to moving on and on balance, you're probably doing good things if you continue to ship things that are showing positive. Right?
turns.zh: 而且就权衡而言，如果你继续 ship 显示正的东西，你大概在做好事？对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. This is awesome. For people that want to run long-term holdout experiments, I imagine you've built your own experimentation system internally? Yeah, we have.
turns.zh: 好。这超棒。对想跑长期 holdout 实验的人，我猜你们内部建了自己的实验系统？对，我们有。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is it basically you hold out 10%, say it was some percentage of users from seeing the new change? Is that how you approach it or is there a different way of approach?
turns.zh: 基本是你 hold out 10%——比如某些比例的用户不看新改动？你们那么做，还是有不同方式？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Two things. We have two layers of holdouts. So one is more the holdouts of every change in a quarter, holdout 5% across the board. Second is for changes that only affect new merchants, what we'll do is we'll take that group of folks, let's call it 50/50 split, and then run that for a few weeks. And then what we're doing, we look at the long-term effects is actually ship the winner to 100%, but we're looking at the cohort of folks who was assigned to the experiment. We're going back and looking at those people who were assigned a year later. (00:21:36): So it allows us to still ship, get stuff out, but we've kind of held the experiment in a way that allows us to see those long-term effects just for the cohort that was exposed. That only works if you're doing it on new users. For existing, it's a little more complicated. That's okay. And then in our experimentation tools, all experimenters are paying that three months, six months, nine months, 12 months with here are the updated results. So you can't really get hide from, what did this really result in over a longer term horizon?
turns.zh: 两件事。我们有两层 holdout。一是每季每个改动的 holdout——全公司 holdout 5%。二是只影响新商家的改动，我们会取那群人，叫它 50/50 分，然后跑几周。然后我们看长期效果的做法是：其实把赢家 ship 到 100%，但我们在看被分配进实验的那批人——我们回头看那些一年前被分配的人。所以它让我们还能 ship、把东西推出去，但我们以某种方式 hold 了实验，让我们可以看到那些被暴露的这批人的长期效果。那只对在新用户上做时 work。对存量用户更复杂。那 OK。然后在我们的实验工具里，所有实验者都被迫在三月、六月、九月、十二月看「这是更新结果」。所以你没法真躲开：这长期视野上到底造成了啥？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your tool is email everyone that's involved with the experiment of here's what this cohort is doing now.
turns.zh: 所以你的工具是邮件所有参与实验的人：这是这批人现在在干啥。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay, that's awesome. It's interesting that you use kind of these cohort curves for GMV, and is that the core metric you look at to see?
turns.zh: 我爱那个。好，那超棒。有趣的是你们用这些 GMV 的 cohort 曲线，那是你们看的核心指标吗？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: There's a few GMV, obviously gross profit. But GMV is kind of like a key determinant of long-term success.
turns.zh: 有几个，GMV、显然还有毛利。但 GMV 是长期成功的关键决定因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's interesting. Most people use cohort retention curves. You're using cohort because you don't look at retention. You're looking at for GMV over time. So that's really interesting.
turns.zh: 有趣。大多数人用 cohort 留存曲线。你们用 cohort 因为你们不看留存——你们看 GMV 随时间。所以那真有趣。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: GMV over time, which correlates better. And there's a retention in profit. And then really the absolute number of merchants who are on the platform and then reaching certain GMV.
turns.zh: GMV 随时间，相关性更好。还有利润的留存。然后真有在平台上的商家绝对数量、以及达到某 GMV 的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I'm going to not keep falling this path. We can go on and on. While we're in the topic of experiments and what you've done, I'm curious if there's any examples of big wins that your team has shipped that might inspire people as they're thinking about launching experiments. I know there's probably some trade secret stuff you don't want competitors to know, and I know this is particular to Shopify and a platform in eCommerce. But I guess is there anything that would be worth sharing of like, "Here's a huge win that maybe we didn't expect."
turns.zh: 好，我不继续这条路了。我们能一直聊。趁我们在实验和你们做了啥的话题，我好奇有没有你们团队 ship 的大赢家例子，能启发人们想 launch 实验。我知道有些 trade secret 你不想让竞争者知道，而且我知道这特定于 Shopify 和电商平台。但有没有值得分享的「这里有个我们没料到的大赢家」？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Going back, there's always a lot of value in thinking through monetary friction as I mentioned. That's always going to be something to export. Trial dynamics, different types of incentives, all of those things are very impactful. (00:23:39): I would say on things that are maybe more practical and for everyone, there's an enormous amount, and we do see these with long-term effects. But just the nuts and bolts of sign up, collecting the right information. And you usually want to collect more information than most people think you do in your sign up flow. If you can then leverage that to personalize the guidance. And this is for SaaS product, the guidance that someone can get when they onboard into Shopify. (00:24:09): So whether you're coming on, Shopify is a very diverse product, in-person selling, online selling different channels. There's the nuts and bolts of get more information from folks, build trust in there, give them right amount of guidance when they come on in a personalized way. (00:24:25): And that may sound like, okay, that's kind of obvious. But the amount of impact by just nailing those flows has never ceased to amaze me and setting up that person for long-term success. So monetary friction. Then just really good onboarding, personalization, a well of opportunities there.
turns.zh: 回到前面，想货币摩擦总有很多价值，如我提的。那永远是可出口的。试用动态、不同类型的激励，都极有影响。我会说对更实际、对所有人适用的东西，有大量——而且我们看到那些有长期效果——就是注册的 nuts and bolts、收集对的信息。你通常想收集比大多数人以为的在注册流里更多的信息。如果你能 leverage 那个去个性化引导。这是对 SaaS 产品、人进 Shopify 时能得到的引导。无论你是来做线下卖、线上卖不同渠道——那些 nuts and bolts：从人那拿更多信息、建立信任、以个性化方式给他们对量的引导。那可能听起来「嗯 obvious」。但光是把那些流做对的影响，从未停止让我惊讶——把那人设为长期成功。所以货币摩擦。然后就是真好的 onboarding、个性化，一大池机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that onboarding comes up every time I ask anyone where they've seen ongoing success and opportunities, particularly in actually surprisingly driving retention. It's interesting that that's not what you look at, but it turns out that's one of the biggest levers for increasing retention. Interesting that even for a company that doesn't look at retention, that's a big opportunity.
turns.zh: 我爱 onboarding 每次我问任何人哪里看到持续成功和机会都冒出来，尤其 surprising 地驱动留存。有趣的是那不是你们看的，但结果那是最增留存的大杠杆之一。有趣的是即便对不看留存的公司，那也是大机会。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yes. Yeah, it's really because it's setting people up, for Shopify's case, I think the big thing about all of our metrics is... What we get very nervous about is the easiest way to increase retention is always to constrict the funnel stage one above the retention metric you're trying to optimize for. (00:25:27): The simplest way to increase my signup to activated thing is just make it harder to sign up. Nuts and bolts, that will always happen is when you have teams on that local conversion rates, you get all these weird team incentives, because they're optimizing to basically implicitly make it harder to do the step before them. (00:25:49): And because we focus on that long-term GMV, number of merchants who are successful, orienting every team to think about the total number of people, not the rate, but the total number of people who got to the end of their part of the journey is a very powerful way to incentivize people to do the right thing in terms of getting people set up versus do the, "I'm going to constrict the funnel step right before me to make my local conversion rate look better," which is the bane of my existence but something I see a lot of teams, implicitly or explicitly do when they get too focused on rates as a way to think about the world.
turns.zh: 对。是的，真因为那是给人 setup。Shopify 的情况，我觉得我们所有指标的大事是……我们非常紧张的是：增留存最容易的方式，总是收紧你优化的那个留存指标上面一步的漏斗阶段。增我的「注册到激活」最简单的方式就是让注册更难。Nuts and bolts，那总发生——当团队在局部转化率上，你会得到所有奇怪的团队激励，因为他们隐式地在让他们的上一步更难。因为我们聚焦长期 GMV、成功的商家数量，把每个团队导向想「到达他们旅程那段结尾的总人数」——不是比率，而是到达那的总人数——是激励人做对的事（让人 setup）的极强方式，vs 做「我要收紧我前面的漏斗步让我的局部转化率好看」——那是我 existence 的 bane（克星），但我看到很多团队隐式或显式地做，当他们太聚焦比率作为看世界的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incentives. What a power.
turns.zh: 激励。多大的力量。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Incentives, what a power, what a lever.
turns.zh: 激励，多大的力量，多大的杠杆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely want to chat a little bit more about metrics. I know you have a really interesting take that's kind of built on what you're just talking about. But first of all, you mentioned this term monetary friction as one of the levers that you've seen success with. Can you just describe what that actually means?
turns.zh: 我 definite 想多聊点指标。我知道你有个建立在你刚说的上面的、很有趣的看法。但首先，你提了「货币摩擦」这个词作为你看到成功的杠杆之一。能描述那到底啥意思吗？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Totally. So things like trial, trial dynamics, trial length, trial amount. It means incentives. So what is in your product? What do people value and need in order to be successful? So in Shopify's case, that might be app score credits or things like that, but those are the two forms of monetary friction we talk about and then of course actual price point. But that's what the larger bucket of monetary friction is.
turns.zh: 完全。像试用、试用动态、试用长度、试用金额。它意思是激励。所以你产品里有啥？人们为了成功价值和需要啥？Shopify 的情况，可能是 app 积分 credit 之类的，但那是我们聊的两种货币摩擦形式，然后当然还有实际价格点。但那是货币摩擦的大桶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's follow this thread of metrics. You're big on absolute numbers and you've been talking about this already, versus percentages and ratios. Talk about that and how you encourage your teams to think about metrics.
turns.zh: 所以让我们跟这个指标线。你 big on 绝对数 (absolute numbers)——你一直在聊这个——vs 百分比和比率。聊那个，以及你怎么鼓励团队想指标。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, I think one of the things that I think happens particularly in large, in Shopify's growth order, it's about 600 folks. When you have teams naturally break up the world into different funnel stages or different points in the journey, it gets very seductive to look at my part of the funnel, and what's my conversion rate through that part of the funnel? And then the team starts to optimize for that conversion rate as their north star over a longer time period. I'm going to try to move my conversion rate from 10 to 12% or what have you. (00:28:04): But in practice, I talked about it's actually almost always easier to just make it harder to do the thing right before your step in the funnel to increase your conversion rate. If I make it harder to sign up, it's going to be very easy to increase sign up to activated rate, because I just have fewer people and the people who made it through our higher intent. (00:28:23): And so I see teams get really stuck when they are trying to optimize conversion rate, but they just make it harder to do the previous thing. Versus everyone is thinking about absolute number of people who made it through their "stage" of the funnel. So instead of I'm trying to convert a bunch of people, a conversion rate, I just want more people to get activated. (00:28:48): And then once you start thinking that way, you realize actually the best way to get more people to get to a step sometimes, and often they just get more people in the door in the first place. So make it easier to sign up or reduce friction. It's the opposite. (00:29:05): Because that will always hurt your conversion rate, but it may actually give you more people on the outside. And a lot of teams get very nervous, their retention rate went down, their LTV went down. Oh my goodness, is this this going to affect our ability to pay? No, your CAC also went down by probably more. And so now you have the ability to likely spend more and you have more people through the door, getting to each point in the activation or the immersion journeys.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得发生在大组织里的事——Shopify 增长组织大概 600 人——当团队自然把世界拆成不同漏斗阶段或旅程节点，会非常有诱惑去看「我的漏斗部分、我这段的转化率」，然后团队开始把那个转化率当长期北极星优化。我想把我的转化率从 10% 移到 12% 或 whatever。但实际上，我聊过，几乎总是更容易的是：让你漏斗里你这步之前的那步更难做来增你的转化率。如果我让注册更难，增「注册到激活」率会非常容易，因为我只是有更少的人、穿过的人意图更高。所以我看到团队卡住当他们想优化转化率，但他们只是让前一步更难。而每个人在想「穿过他们漏斗『阶段』的绝对人数」。所以与其我想转化一堆人、一个转化率，我更想要更多人被激活。一旦你开始那么想，你意识到其实让更多人到某步的最好方式有时、而且常常是就一开始让更多人进门。所以让注册更容易或降摩擦。那是相反的。因为那永远伤你的转化率，但它可能真给你门外更多人。很多团队非常紧张他们的留存率降了、LTV 降了。哦我的天，这会影响我们付费能力吗？不，你的 CAC 也大概降更多。所以现在你大概能花更多、你有更多人进门，到达 ea——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing is essentially teams are gold not on increase, lift this conversion step by some percentage. It's drive some absolute number of new merchants, potentially.
turns.zh: 我听到的基本是团队 not 在「增、把这转化步提几个百分点」，而是驱动某个绝对数的新商家，可能。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Merchants, yeah. Exactly.
turns.zh: 商家，对。Exact。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to I want to hear how you structure your growth team at Shopify. Essentially, what's the raw structure, what are the different teams, and what do they focus on? And then what are the functions within each teams?
turns.zh: 这是接去我想听你们怎么结构增长团队的好 segue。本质上，原始结构啥、不同团队是啥、他们聚焦啥？然后每个团队里的职能是啥？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: We have two big groups within growth. So one is what we call growth R&D. So this might be what you traditionally consider product design engineering, data, your traditional product teams. Then we have growth marketing, which in Shopify's case is paid acquisition, media buying, affiliate marketing, email, content, and SEO. So that's growth R&D, growth marketing. (00:30:23): Within growth R&D, three pillars. One is what we call growth products. And so this is basically everything from landing pages, sign up, onboarding, monetization. So trial, incentives, the like, all the way through to what we call our home feed, our engagement to basically get more merchants. Again, not necessarily to retain, but to keep giving entrepreneurship a try to become bigger and bigger businesses. So that's growth product, the full life cycle there. (00:30:56): Second is what we call our enable pillar, and this pillar is building tools for both growth and the rest of Shopify. So things like experimentation platform, our communication platform, our business intelligence tooling that powers a lot of what we're doing, our more tech work to support our growth marketing team. (00:31:14): And then our third bucket, which is maybe a little different from most growth teams is actually our customer support, groups within growth. We want to think about customer support as part of this merchant journey of coming on, giving entrepreneurship a try, all the way through to here's the support I need as I'm becoming a multi-billion dollar business on Shopify. So those are the three big growth product buckets. And then within growth marketing, it's a more traditional channel setup. Paid, all the different channels online, offline, SEO, email, and affiliates.
turns.zh: 增长里我们有两个大组。一是我们叫增长 R&D。这可能是你传统认为的产品、设计、工程、数据、你的传统产品团队。然后我们有增长营销 (growth marketing)——Shopify 的情况是付费获取、媒体购买、联盟营销、邮件、内容、SEO。所以那是增长 R&D、增长营销。增长 R&D 里，三根柱子。一是我们叫增长产品 (growth products)。基本是从落地页、注册、onboarding、变现——试用、激励之类——一路到我们叫主页信息流 (home feed)、我们的互动——基本去 get 更多商家。again，不一定为了留存，而是为了持续给创业一个试、变成越来越大的业务的机会。所以那是增长产品，那边的全生命周期。二是我们叫赋能 (enable) 柱子，这柱子是给增长和 Shopify 其他部分建工具。像实验平台、我们的沟通平台、我们的商业智能工具（驱动我们很多东西）、支持我们增长营销团队的更多技术工作。三是我们第三桶——可能跟大多数增长团队有点不同——其实是我们客户支持 (customer support) 里在增长里的组。我们想让客户支持作为这商家旅程的一部分来想：从进来、给创业一个试，一路到「当我变成 Shopify 上数十亿的业务时我需要的支持」。所以那是增长产品的三大桶。然后增长营销里是更传统的渠道设置。付费、所有不同线上线下渠道、SEO、邮件、联盟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. Okay. So within growth RD, I just took notes. I'm going to summarize what you just shared, which is awesome. So there's three big buckets. One is growth product, which essentially is onboarding. It feels like it's like the top of funnel, get people in. Well okay, so growth marketing feels like that's super top of funnel bring-
turns.zh: 超酷。好。所以在增长 R&D 里，我刚记了笔记。我要总结你刚分享的，超棒。所以有三桶。一是增长产品，基本是 onboarding。感觉像漏斗顶部、把人带进来。嗯好，增长营销感觉像那是超顶部漏斗带——

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: That's super top funnel.
turns.zh: 那是超顶部漏斗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, got it. So growth marketing, drive people to Shopify.com. Then within RD team, growth product takes that user and tries to get them to activate it. Enable helps... It feels like that's like internal tooling and ways to make the teams internally more efficient.
turns.zh: 对。好，懂了。所以增长营销把人带到 Shopify.com。然后在 R&D 团队里，增长产品拿那个用户、试图让他们激活。赋能帮……感觉像内部工具化和让内部团队更高效的方式。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct. Both growth and outside growth.
turns.zh: 对。增长里和外头增长都。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. And then the customer support team, that's really interesting. So there's a customer support product team that helps new merchants be successful. And does that include actual customer support agents? Is that within that team?
turns.zh: 超棒。好。然后客户支持团队，真有趣。所以有客户支持产品团队帮新商家成功。那包括实际的客户支持 agent 吗？在那团队里？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: That's not. We build a tooling to make those support advisors superheroes. And then on the help center, all of our AI stuff to make a great customer experience for people who are just engaging in a self-serve. So it's the tooling and the experience for merchants.
turns.zh: 不包括。我们建工具化让那些支持顾问变超级英雄。然后在帮助中心，我们所有 AI 东西给自助的人极好的客户体验。所以那是给商家的工具化和体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So with these teams, is there anything you can share about just how you think about metrics/goals for these different buckets? We don't need to get too deeply, but does everyone basically have an absolute new merchants goal or is it a little different?
turns.zh: 好。对这些团队，有没有能分享的你们怎么想这些不同桶的指标/目标？不用太深，但大家基本都有个绝对新商家目标，还是有点不同？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: So yeah. So at the highest level we think about that total cohort value. We bring in a set of merchants in a given year. How much GMV, how much that set of merchants worth over the next three, four years to Shopify? And that's the most important thing that we want to focus on. And then that of course, from an efficiency standpoint, that of course meeting our payback guardrails and all of that. So that's the macro growth perspective. Cohort value over cost and payback. So that's the macro point of view. (00:33:52): And then within growth marketing, each channel operates with certain guardrails around their LTV CACs. Same thing for content and SEO. That operates with kind of a guardrail model for each piece of content. How much is that going to come back and down the line? (00:34:09): For growth products, it's also a combination of total GP incremental cohort value that's produced from those teams. So everything is basically going to be measured on from an experiment, ideally measured over a very long time period. What was the incremental cohort value lift that this generated? And that's how we think about and measure the impact of each of those sub teams along the way. (00:34:40): Each of those have a civic part of the funnel they play with. But because they're measured on absolutes and they really think about that absolute value, we don't get caught into, did your conversion rate over the course of this year go up or down? It's kind of irrelevant. What was the sum of the impact over a long period on that total cohort value that we're trying to produce from before merchants?
turns.zh: 对。所以最高层我们想那个总 cohort 价值。我们一年带进一批商家。那批商家在接下来三、四年对 Shopify 值多少 GMV？那是我们最想聚焦的最重要的事。然后从效率角度，当然满足我们的回收 guardrail 之类。所以那是宏观增长视角。Cohort 价值对成本和回收。那是宏观视角。然后增长营销里，每个渠道用某些围绕他们 LTV/CAC 的 guardrail 运作。内容和 SEO 同——每个内容用一种 guardrail 模型。那内容长期回来多少？增长产品里，也是那些团队产的总 GP（毛利）增量 cohort 价值的组合。所以一切基本从实验测——理想在很长时段测——这生成的增量 cohort 价值 lift 是啥？那是我们想、测每个子团队沿途影响的方式。每个有他们玩的漏斗公民部分。但因为他们在绝对数上测、真想那个绝对值，我们不会陷进「你今年转化率升了还是降了？」那有点无关。重要的是：在我们要从新商家产出的总 cohort 价值上，长期的总影响之和是多少？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the way you come up with this goal I imagine is you have a forecast of where things would go organically, and then here's the lift we want to see from the work this team does this quarter, this year.
turns.zh: 你们定这目标的方式我猜是你们有有机会去哪的 forecast，然后这是这团队这季、这年想看到的 lift。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct. And then we're going to measure against for each experiment, did it actually get to where we expect that lift to be?
turns.zh: 对。然后我们会针对每个实验测：它真到我们预期那个 lift 了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And those experiments again, are those all long-term holdout experiments where you look wait a year or some-
turns.zh: 而那些实验，again，都是你们看等一年或更长的长期 holdout 实验？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: We call. We call the experiment after three weeks, but in all cases, the group is held, we watch them. And that's where that ping comes back, every experiment is watched. And that ping comes back three, six months, 12 months to re-look at was this actually successful?
turns.zh: 我们叫。我们三周后叫实验，但在所有 case，那组被 hold，我们看着他们。那就是那个 ping 回来的地方——每个实验被看。那 ping 在三、六、十二月回来，重看这真成功了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好，酷。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: So that creates the loop of shipping value quickly, but making sure we're holding ourselves accountable to did this actually produce results over a long period, or did it actually just have this neutral effect? It's like, oh, then we can learn from that and get better.
turns.zh: 所以那创造了快速 ship 价值的循环，但确保我们对自己负责——这真在长期产结果了吗，还是其实只是中性效果？像，哦，那我们能从那学、变更好。

turns.en: 30. Yeah.

turns.en: Yeah. Okay, so it's still roughly, yeah.
