turns.zh: 而那是超棒的学习，那是我们拿它的原因。像，哇好，现在我们真揭开东西了，那是如此成功的发现。哇好，我们以为这东西。但现在学到它其实没我们以为的真。酷。我们能从那拿啥、下次更聪明，不 just double down 在错的东西上？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. And again, and you mentioned most of the reason this is the case when something doesn't show lift down the road is it's pulling forward success that would've been seen later on its own if you had not even shipped this thing?
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。again，你提大多数这情况的原因——当事情下游不显示 lift——是它把本来会自己后来看到的成功「提前拉动」了，如果你甚至没 ship 这东西？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Is there an example by any chance that comes to mind of something like that that's just like, "Wow, that was a big win. And then oh I see we just pulled forward some revenue from the future."
turns.zh: 超棒。有没有这样的例子，就「哇，那是个大赢家。然后哦我看到了我们只是从未来拉了点收入」？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: So I think one good example is something around payment failure notifications. So one of the things that a lot of teams have or see is we call Dunning effects where somebody might have a payment not go through, a credit card that doesn't go through. So we did a bunch of experimentation around, hey, how can we alert people that their credit card is failed, their payment attempt failed? (00:38:47): And that's a typical growth win, usually produces a lot of short-term impact. And that's what we saw here. We were doing much better alerting, reminding people, sending them a million emails about it. Cool, we got some pretty major lift. (00:38:59): You look back six, 12 months. There was really no long-term lift. And why is that? Because there's really a little bit of a selection bias there that people who were letting that payment fail probably weren't actually that dedicated to this entrepreneurship craft. They may have updated their credit card, but they still really weren't in it. (00:39:22): And so that was a good example of in a bunch of this stuff around payments, even "preventing" churn where you look, it's six, 12, 18 months. On a GMV metric, not a lot of lift over that long-term horizon.
turns.zh: 我觉得好例子是围绕支付失败通知 (payment failure notifications) 的。很多团队有或看到的——我们叫 Dunning 效应——某人的支付没过、信用卡没过。所以我们做了一堆实验：嘿，我们怎么提醒人们他们的信用卡失败了、支付尝试失败？那是典型增长赢家，通常产很多短期影响。我们在这看到了。我们更好 alert、提醒人们、发一百万封邮件。酷，我们拿到相当大 lift。你看回六、十二月。其实没有长期 lift。为啥？因为那有点选择偏差——让支付失败的人可能其实没那么投入到这创业手艺。他们可能更新了信用卡，但他们仍不真在里面。所以那是好例子：在支付这堆事里，即便「防止」churn——你看六、十二、十八月——在 GMV 指标上，长期视野没多少 lift。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this example. I could see so many people having run experiments like this and like, "Oh, we found such a huge win. This team's killing it. What a great idea. Of course this makes sense," and then turns out it's nothing long term.
turns.zh: 我爱这例子。我能看到这么多人跑过这种实验、「哦我们找到这么大赢家。这队 kill 它。多好的点子。当然这说得通」，然后结果长期啥也不是。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Which is great. We were going to spend a lot of time, okay, what else can we do here? It's like, no actually bigger fish to fry in a lot of other areas. So it helps the team just feel really good that their work is really the things that were good. (00:40:13): Another one that went the other way, which was really interesting was in our online store, and this might be if you use Shopify, we have sections and blocks that come pre-configured. And so we tested, okay, if we give you a pre-configured block of you should have an image up top, then a text banner, and then a collage with your products. That should help folks understand what to do when they're building the online store. It actually had no lift in people converting to a paying merchant. (00:40:48): However, when we looked longer term on that six months later, it had a pretty massive impact on the number of people who were selling and producing GMV. And why is that? Because it didn't likely really influence anyone to buy Shopify or pay for Shopify. But the people who used it created better stores that were higher converting, and so they got early sales. They actually converted one of their visitors and they got momentum, and they stuck with entrepreneurship a little bit longer. And we saw that in that opposite way. (00:41:21): And so this is an example where that neutral, and so we tend to ship neutral. It's like it could be positive and so let's let it go if we have good intuition about it and it'll turn. So we've seen a bunch of these things go in very different directions.
turns.zh: 那是好的。我们本来要花很多时间「好，这里还能做啥？」像，不，其实更大鱼在别处炸。所以那帮团队就感觉真好——他们的工作真是那些好的东西。另一个走相反方向的、真有趣的是在我们的在线商店——如果你用 Shopify 你知道，我们有预配置的 sections 和 blocks。我们测了：好，如果我们给你预配置的 block——你该顶部放图、然后文字 banner、然后你产品的拼贴——那该帮人理解建在线商店时干啥。它对变成付费商家其实没 lift。然而，我们看长期——六个月后——它对「在卖、产 GMV 的人数」有相当大影响。为啥？因为它不太可能真影响任何人买 Shopify 或付费。但用了它的人建了更好的店、更高转化，所以他们拿到早期销售。他们其实转化了一个访客、拿到动量、他们在创业上多坚持了会。我们在那相反方向看到。所以这是中性的例子——我们倾向 ship 中性。像它可能正、所以如果我们对它有好直觉就让它走，它会转。所以我们看到一堆这些事走非常不同的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so fascinating. I didn't realize that you ship neutral experiments. That's an interesting insight. So it's like if you feel good about it and it's neutral, you ship it?
turns.zh: 这太迷人了。我不知道你们 ship 中性实验。那是有趣的洞察。所以像如果你对它感觉好、它是中性，你就 ship？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: In our culture of the kind of aim heavy, if the intuition is right that this probably is helping merchants, why do we start with that the original control is better if it's neutral? Let's start with, what would we have shipped if we were a blank slate? And if it's neutral, actually neither is better, so let's just pick the one we feel better about and ship that.
turns.zh: 在我们的 aim heavy（重瞄准）文化里，如果直觉对——这大概在帮商家——为啥我们从原控制更好开始，如果它是中性？让我们从「如果是白纸我们会 ship 啥」开始。如果中性，其实都不更好，所以就挑我们感觉更好的那个 ship。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes so much sense. Oh man. Okay, so let's talk about this a little bit more. So this aim heavy concept, this idea of thinking 100 years out, can you just share more about that insight and that philosophy? I know it sounds like it comes from Tobi of how he likes to think about the business.
turns.zh: 太说得通了。哦老天。好，所以我们多聊这个。这 aim heavy 概念、这想 100 年外的想法，能多分享那洞察和哲学吗？我知道它听起来来自 Tobi 他怎么想生意。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Totally. It is all Tobi of really making sure Shopify is so oriented around, we are here to build 100 year company. And so the decisions we're going to make are really oriented towards the long-term success of merchants, of Shopify. Embedded in all of our principles are make the best product in the world, make money to do more of one. Never reverse principles two and three. In every kind of executive meeting, every town hall, that slide comes up. It's like you've been at Shopify, you've probably seen that slide 10,000 times. But it's an important reminder job is to build the best product for merchants over the long period of time. And then all of the metrics and the make money part of it, secondary to that. So what we care about is that long term piece. It ties a little bit to that original conversation about entrepreneurs and being the core of why we just want more people to start businesses and go. (00:43:15): It's very seductive I think in most companies, including in Shopify because we can support large enterprise businesses today, right? Big brands who want to get off an outdated solution and come over to Shopify. It's very easy to just say, "Oh, that's very concrete." There's an existing business, we want to have them come join Shopify. (00:43:40): And in the short term it feels really good. It brings a lot of revenue right away. But if you're thinking about the long-term 100 years from now, guess what? All of the big brands of today be out of business. And many of them will be out of business in 30, 40, 50 years. The real success of Shopify is getting every business to start with us and go, but making that type of an investment and being so focused on that entrepreneur segment and making it easier is how we build a very, very long-term oriented company. So just even how we do capital investment, how we do product decision-making comes back to, hey, we can't chase the short-term. Even more concrete things.
turns.zh: 完全。它全 Tobi 的——真确保 Shopify 如此 oriented around 我们在这建 100 年公司。所以我们做的决定真 oriented 商家、Shopify 的长期成功。嵌在我们所有原则里的是「建世界上最好的产品、赚钱做更多之一、永不反转原则二和三」。每个高管会、每个 town hall，那 slide 出来。你在 Shopify 大概看过那 slide 一万次。但那是重要提醒：工作是建对商家长期最好的产品。然后所有指标和赚钱部分，次要于那个。所以我们 care 的是长期那块。它连回最早那关于创业者的对话、为啥我们就是想更多人开始业务并走。在大多数公司——包括 Shopify，因为我们今天能支持大企业——很诱惑就说「哦那很具体。有个现有业务，我们想让他们来 Shopify」。短期感觉真好，立刻带很多收入。但如果你想长期 100 年，猜怎么着？今天所有大品牌都会不在了。很多会在 30、40、50 年不在。Shopify 的真成功是让每个业务从我们开始并走，但做那种投资、如此聚焦那创业者细分、让它更容易，是我们建非常长期 oriented 公司的方式。所以即便更具体的东西——我们怎么做资本投资、怎么做产品决策——都回到「嘿我们不能追短期」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that comes to mind where you did that where something short-term looked like, "We should definitely do this," but we're thinking thinking 100 years out so we're going to approach it this way?
turns.zh: 有没有例子你那么做——某短期看起来「我们 definite 该做这个」，但我们想 100 年外所以我们用这方式 approach？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: It's kind of very much just imbued in the culture. Almost everything kind of feels that way. And I'll give, practically speaking, every six weeks all the R&D group leads we get together and we sit with Tobi and each other and review every single project across the company. Every six weeks, every single R&D pull up the dashboard, and look at it. (00:44:56): And in that conversation, so much of the conversation is about both the technical how. How are we building this in a way that allows for Shopify to have optionality in the technical decisions that we are making? And I think for Tobi, one of the things I've learned and so is that how, the technical architecture determines strategy in a technology company even more than the what and who we're building for. If you build the right technical how and set yourself up to have a platform that can be adaptable, flexible, that is incredibly valuable over the long term. It means we will sometimes take longer to ship a feature. It means we'll not chase certain deals or what have you, but we're going to kind of make that investment. And it comes through in all of our reviews and just how we got to do our work together.
turns.zh: 它 kind of 非常 imbued 在文化里。几乎一切都那感觉。我给个实际的：每六周所有 R&D 组 lead 聚一起、跟 Tobi 和彼此坐、review 公司每个项目。每六周，每个 R&D 拉起 dashboard 看。在那对话里，很多是关于「怎么」(how) 的技术——我们怎么建这、让 Shopify 在技术决策上有选择权？我觉得对 Tobi，我学到的一件事是：在科技公司，「怎么」——技术架构——比「什么」和「为谁建」更决定战略。如果你建对的技术 how、让自己有个可适应、灵活的平台，那长期极有价值。意思是我们有时会花更久 ship 一个功能。意思是我们不追某些单子或 whatever，但我们要做那种投资。它贯穿我们所有 review、我们怎么一起工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is really unique. I've not heard of that where how... Usually it's the opposite. Let's not worry about how we're going to build this thing. It's why are we building this thing and then when are we building it? And not just the architecture is the most important thing.
turns.zh: 哇，那真独特。我没听过 where how……通常相反。别担心我们怎么建这东西。是 why 我们建这东西、然后 when 我们建。不是架构最重要。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, I mean in the last one, it was great. We had a 30-minute discussion about how to build CSV importers for people coming over from different platforms, and it was all about are we using open source library, doing it internally, are we doing it in the core code base? Are we building a separate first party app to do it? It was incredible detail. (00:46:29): This is what's amazing about Tobi. The technical detail of how we're going to do this was incredibly important to get right, to kind of set up this type of infrastructure. And most companies it'd be okay what, you're going to make it easier for people to migrate their data over. Cool. Team, go figure out how. And if team does figure out the how do we work on it with Tobi and the details, because the how is so important to how we build for the future.
turns.zh: 对。我的意思是最后一个，超棒。我们有 30 分钟讨论怎么建 CSV importer 给从别的平台来的人，全是关于用开源库、内部做、在核心代码库做、还是建个独立第一方 app 做。细节惊人。这是 Tobi 惊人的地方。我们怎么做的那技术细节对错极重要，去设那种基础设施。大多数公司会「OK 啥，你要让搬数据更容易。酷。团队去搞清楚 how」。而如果团队搞清 how 我们跟 Tobi 和细节工作，因为 how 对我们为未来建多重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's fascinating. And usually it's how do we do this as quick as possible, because CVS importing is not our core differentiator. It'll just build something good enough, we'll ship it, we'll move on.
turns.zh: 那迷人。通常它是「我们怎么尽快做，因为 CSV 导入不是我们核心差异化。就建个够好的，ship，move on」。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Totally the opposite. That is fascinating. What's also really interesting about this is I think about Brian Chesky at Airbnb where I worked for a while and his... So one, he also had this idea of the 100-year vision and thinking for the future way out in 100 years. But interestingly, since he's a designer, he had a very different focus. So Tobi, he was an engineer. He still codes from what I can see on Twitter, he still-
turns.zh: 完全相反。那迷人。这也很有趣的是我想到 Airbnb 的 Brian Chesky——我在那工作一阵——他的……一，他也有这 100 年愿景、想未来 100 年。但有趣的是，因为他是设计师，他有非常不同的聚焦。Tobi 是工程师。我从 Twitter 看还在写代码、还——

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I could see why his brain goes there and why he's really strong in the how. Brian on the other hand is very focused on the experience and making sure the design is amazing, and the app is exactly what he wants it to feel like. It is very experience oriented. So it's interesting that these founders lean into the thing that they're strong at, and understand deeply, and that ideally connects with the way this business specifically wins and grows. And it makes sense a platform, I could see why engineering would be so essential to get right. Travel, hospitality, consumer app. I could see why design is so important.
turns.zh: 所以我能看为啥他脑去那、为啥他在 how 上真强。Brian 另一方面非常聚焦体验和确保设计惊艳、app 正是他要的感觉。非常体验 oriented。所以有趣的是这些创始人 lean into 他们强的东西、深度理解的东西、而那 ideal 连着这生意具体怎么赢和成长。而说得通：平台，我能看为啥工程如此关键要对。旅游、 hospitality、消费者 app，我能看为啥设计如此重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. One more tidbit that I've heard about how you all think about this is metrics. And you mentioned before we started recording that a lot of the company doesn't actually have metrics that drive what they build, especially within the core business, which I think surprised a lot of people. Most people are like, "Every team needs a metric and a KPI, and this is how we measure progress and this is how we know if they're doing well." Talk about just how that works, how most of the companies doesn't have a metric.
turns.zh: 迷人。我听的另一个 tidbit 是你们怎么想指标。你录音前提到很多公司其实没有驱动他们建什么的指标，尤其核心业务里，我想那惊讶很多人。大多数人「每个团队需要个指标和 KPI，这是我们测进度、知道他们做得好的方式」。聊下那怎么 work、大多数公司没有指标。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah. It's funny, we ran against KPIs are basically banned as OKRs or banned and all that. And so certainly, in growth you have metrics, but they take a different form. And then in core, it truly is, do we have conviction that this is the right technical foundation to build the future of commerce? And that is built through certainly looking at data. So it's not that teams are not looking at data and using it as a piece of their puzzle, but it's not the overriding. And when we go to ship a feature in core, it's not like a team is held accountable for this metric over this six months. It's much more, did we ship the right thing? And we're going to kind of get at that through a variety of lenses. Could be some of that could be data, qualitative, just our own product sense of what's good or not. (00:49:24): And so I think the upside of that is I think we tend to ship things in core and that are incredibly forward-facing and we take more risk. I think to acknowledge some of the downside of it though is sometimes conversations get extremely subjective about what is the right thing to do. And so that requires the right way of having good discussions, openness from all leaders and from teams to debate those things. But it does result in some squishiness, which again has its pros and cons, but taste is what drives a lot of what we're shipping in core.
turns.zh: 对。好玩，我们基本禁 KPI——作为 OKR 或 whatever 禁。所以 certainly 增长里有指标，但形式不同。然后在核心，真就是「我们有 conviction 这是建商务未来的正确技术基础吗？」那当然通过看数据建。所以不是团队不看数据、用它做拼图一块，但它不是 overriding。当我们去 ship 核心功能，不是团队对这六月的这指标负责。更是「我们 ship 了对的东西吗？」我们会用各种 lens 到那——可能是些数据、定性、就我们对啥好啥不好的产品感。所以我认为 upside 是我们在核心倾向 ship 极 forward-facing、我们冒更多险。要承认 downside 是有时对话变得极主观关于啥是对的。所以需要对的讨论方式、所有领导和团队开放去 debate 那些。但它导致一些 squishiness（模糊），again 有 pros and cons，但品味 (taste) 驱动很多我们在核心 ship 的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'm glad you touched on that. I was going to say, okay, everyone would love this idea of just build things that we think are awesome. It's going to be great. But then you build a whole org with teams and people building stuff. How does one know if they're building things that are good and helping versus not? (00:50:21): And you're pointing out there are pros and cons to that. The pros is we're not optimizing for some short-term wins and driving some poor metric. The con is you might ship stuff that... There's a lot of subjectivity, and people may not agree, and it's a lot of squishy stuff.
turns.zh: 对，我高兴你提到那个。我想说，好，人人会爱「就建我们觉得超棒的东西」这想法。但然后你建个整个 org 有团队有人建东西。人怎么知道他们建的东西好、在帮 vs 不？你指出那有 pros and cons。Pro 是我们不为某些短期赢和优化某些差指标。Con 是你可能 ship 些……很多主观性，人们可能不同意，很多 squishy 的东西。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, totally. Glen, who's heads of core product, I mean one of the things that's so impressive about Glen and that core team is they go incredibly deep into every single release that is shipped. And so you do have a central eye on the quality and how it all fits together. (00:51:00): And so that I think helps make sure there's a consistent kind of bar for taste. A bunch of folks Tobi obviously that can enforce that. So it's subjective, but it's objective in the sense that it's kind of a small number of people who really hold what that bar is and needs to be. I think if it's just subjective, let's just ship what we want without a couple people really holding that quality and that taste bar, that's where things go really sideways.
turns.zh: 对，完全。Glen——核心产品头——我和那核心团队一件超 impressive 的事是他们极深地进每个 ship 的 release。所以你确实有个中央眼在质量、和所有怎么 fit 一起。所以那我觉帮确保有个一致的品味 bar。一堆人——Tobi obviously——能 enforce 那个。所以它主观，但在「少数真正 hold 那 bar 是啥、需要时是啥」的意义上客观。如果就主观、让我们 ship 我们要的、没几个人真 hold 那质量和品味 bar，那才是事情真 sideways 的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's exactly what I was going to ask is, who's the ultimate decider of taste and what is good? And so it sounds like basically Tobi above, and then he's kind of deputized Glen and relies on him to make a lot of these final calls. And then I imagine Glen has some folks that he kind of deputizes to make smaller decisions along the way. Or not, or he's very involved in everything.
turns.zh: 超棒。那正是我想问的——谁最终决定品味、啥是好？所以听起来基本 Tobi 在上，然后他 kind of 授权 Glen、依赖他做很多这些最终 call。然后我猜 Glen 有些他授权做小决定的人沿途。或不是，或他非常参与一切。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: And I think this is the fun thing about Shopify. Literally we have our own internal project management system that's been kind of crafted just for Shopify and every shift-
turns.zh: 我觉得这是 Shopify 好玩的事。我们真有自己的内部项目管理系统，为 Shopify 定制，每个 shift——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that called by the way? It's got a cool name, right?
turns.zh: 那叫啥来着？有个酷名字，对吧？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: GSD.
turns.zh: GSD。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: GSD, yeah. [inaudible 00:52:10].
turns.zh: GSD，对。[inaudible]

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, get it done.
turns.zh: 对，get shit done（把事干完）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I remember.
turns.zh: 那是我记得的。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: So get shit done. And every project, so you got a core project, you have emergency service, you got growth project. And the expectation is that the group leads. Every single project that goes out has a few minute video with Figmas and everything, and everything that shipped. Needs to be okay-toed, so approved by the group lead. There's nothing that can ship without that okay-to approval. And that okay-to approval has to be Glen, Carl, myself with different groups. And so that is how everything is reviewed. Now of course there's great amazing teams that do amazing work, but it is that that's how the system works.
turns.zh: 所以每个项目——核心项目、紧急服务、增长项目——期望是组 lead。每个 ship 的项目都有个几分钟视频带 Figma 和一切、和所有 ship 的。需要 okay-toed，即被组 lead 批准。没那 okay-to 批准啥都不能 ship。而那 okay-to 批准得是 Glen、Carl、我（不同组）。所以那是一切怎么 review 的。当然有超棒的团队做超棒工作，但那就是系统怎么 work。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And okay-to specifically means someone above reviews it or all this whole team, everyone looks at it?
turns.zh: 而 okay-to 具体意思是某人 above review 它、还是整个团队所有人都看？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: No. So Glen reviews the core stuff. Carl reviews the MS. Okay-to. It's interesting.
turns.zh: 不。Glen review 核心的东西。Carl review MS（商家服务）的 okay-to。有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's basically Glen is founder mode and not as a founder where he's involved in all the details, has final say. So this is a really cool example of founder mode, but not as a founder.
turns.zh: 基本 Glen 是 founder mode——不是作为创始人、而是他参与所有细节、有最终 say。所以这是 founder mode 的好例子，但不是作为创始人。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the way you guys operate. And I imagine sometimes Tobi disagrees with Glen and then they talk about it and things get ironed out.
turns.zh: 在你们运作的方式里。我猜有时 Tobi 不同意 Glen，然后他们聊、事情熨平。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Totally. And that's why we come together every six weeks, everyone in person to review every project so we can hash out those disagreements. Go through all the core projects, all the merge service projects, all the growth projects. And it's a great forum to say, "Hey, here's where we disagree," really on the how and the tactics of what's happening. And we can flag those things, have good debates about whether there might be misalignment.
turns.zh: 完全。那是为什么我们每六周聚一起、所有人线下 review 每个项目，我们能 hash out 那些分歧。过所有核心项目、所有合并服务项目、所有增长项目。那是说「嘿，这是我们不同意的地方」的好论坛——真在 how 和战术上——我们能 flag 那些、有好的 debate 关于是不是有 misalignment。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What a unique way of working. I'm so fascinated by all this. So what I'm hearing essentially within Core, Glen and his team come up with, "Here's what we're going to build the next quarter." You guys have twice a year releases, is that right? Or is it every season?
turns.zh: 惊人。多独特的工作方式。我被所有这些迷住。所以我听到的基本是，在核心里，Glen 和他团队出「下季我们要建啥」。你们一年两次 release，对吧？还是每季？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, so big additions. Twice a year. Obviously continually shipping, but we package them twice a year in a big bang.
turns.zh: 对，大添加，一年两次。显然持续 ship，但我们一年两次打包成大 bang。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Big launch. Yep, I've seen those. Okay. So he's like, "Here's what we're going to do in the next release. We're just going to build this because we think this is right. And we're not driving a specific goal. We're building for 100 years in the future. Let's just build it." And basically you build it. He's like, "This is great, not great, iterate until it's this good," and then ship. And great. Okay, this is great. Okay, so then there's that team, and then there's your team, which is drive some freaking numbers, drive growth, hit these goals. How do you collaborate across these two teams? Do you have a model for how you work together? Because these feel like very different ways of working?
turns.zh: 大 launch。对，我看过那些。好。所以他说「下个 release 我们要做啥。我们就建这个因为我们觉得这对。我们不在驱动特定目标。我们为 100 年未来建。就建。」然后基本你建它。他说「这超棒、不超棒，iterate 直到这么好」，然后 ship。好。好，那是那团队，然后有你团队——驱动一些 freaking 数字、驱动增长、hit 这些目标。你们俩怎么跨这两个团队协作？有你们一起工作的方式吗？因为这些感觉是非常不同的工作方式。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, honestly, it's been one of the things I'm very proud of. We built a really great partnership for the last three and a half years, because it's intentionally meant to be almost at odds, and that's part of the structure of how we want to work. (00:54:56): But it comes from, I think, a place of respect on both sides. And I'd say for anyone, it's okay, here's what growth is going to do. We're going to do it in a way that is high quality, that is shipping really good stuff for merchants. We're probably going to approach it in a faster way. We might disagree on things, but we're going to have reasonable paths to handle that conflict. (00:55:17): And so while there's no magic bullet, it wasn't like these are the surfaces that growth can touch, these are not. It was like you can go anywhere in the product, but let's go figure out how to work together to figure out that quality bar to understand when you're going to be different on it, on the quality bar to get something out to learn, and just building trust along the way that we're actually going to ship high quality things and we ship it to 100% and move. And so a lot of great work on the team to make those relationships really strong.
turns.zh: 对，老实说，那是我非常骄傲的事之一。我们建了真好的 partnership 过去三年半，因为它 intentional 地 meant 几乎对立，那是我们要怎么工作的结构的一部分。但它来自——我觉得——两边的尊重。而对任何人，是 OK：这是增长要做的。我们用高质量方式做、ship 真好的东西给商家。我们可能用更快方式 approach。我们可能在事上不同意，但我们有合理的路径 handle 那冲突。所以虽然没有魔法子弹——不是「这些是增长能碰的表面、这些不是」——是「你能去产品任何地方，但让我们搞清怎么一起工作、搞清那质量 bar、理解当你要在质量 bar 上不同时、为学东西推出去、沿途建信任我们真会 ship 高质量东西、ship 到 100% 然后 move」。所以团队大量好工作让那些关系真强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So basically, you guys are like, "Moving this button over here is going to drive so much growth," and then Glen's like, "No, this is not acceptable. We don't want a button here. This looks terrible. Everyone's going to hate it." So that's the healthy tension. I'm describing a combative-
turns.zh: 明白了。所以基本你们像「把这按钮挪这会驱动这么多增长」，然后 Glen 像「不，这不可接受。我们不想这有个按钮。这看起来糟。人人会恨它」。所以那是健康张力。我描述的是 combative——

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: [inaudible 00:56:01] totally. And it's like, okay, so how are we going to work to figure this out? It might be, "Hey, we're going to move the button. Hey let's run the test," but see the short-term lift. You know we're going to monitor it long term. You know when we ship it, it's going to be high quality, high quality polish. And you trust us to make those trade-offs. (00:56:19): I wish I had a better answer of it's very human. It's very that trust that's that's very important in any of these. I think growth with other teams is like, there's no replacement for just the human trust and then following through on commitments of no, we are actually going to make this thing really good.
turns.zh: [inaudible] 完全。像，好，那我们怎么工作搞清这个？可能「嘿我们要挪按钮。嘿我们跑测试」但看短期 lift。你知道我们会长期监控。你知道我们 ship 它时会高质量、高抛光。你信任我们做那些 trade-off。我希望有更好的答案——它非常 human。就是那信任，在任何这些里非常重要。我觉得增长跟其他团队，没有替代的就是 human 信任、然后跟进承诺「不，我们真会让这东西真好」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that, that comes to mind where you had something that was you thought was going to drive meaningful growth? You showed it to Glenn, he is like, "No, don't know about this." And then either you iterated or you just forget it, this isn't right for the platform even though it's going to drive some meaningful growth?
turns.zh: 有那样的例子吗——你以为会驱动有意义增长的东西？你给 Glen 看，他说「不，不咋确定这个」。然后要么你迭代、要么你就忘了它，不对平台合适、即便它会驱动一些有意义增长？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: The place that we often come back to is, and this is with I think Tobi is great, Tobi and Glen, is on wizards. So wizards-
turns.zh: 我们常回到的地方——我觉得 Tobi 超棒、Tobi 和 Glen——是 wizard（向导）。所以 wizard——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Onboarding carousels.
turns.zh: Onboarding 轮播。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Onboarding carousels. Some way that basically has folks get set up by not using the actual product. And so we've always kind of danced around and we have very specific no wizard principle, but I think that sometimes the tension is wizards can serve a purpose in certain circumstances, but we've avoided doing that. But we've always worked to try to make the principles of what a wizard does really well, which is it simplifies the product into something that allows people to have a lower bar, to try to work with core to bring that into the actual experience itself. (00:57:52): So the example of that experiment I mentioned to you of giving pre-filled sections in the online store editor, you could have solved that in a wizardy way of, "Enter a few things, and we're going to generate these sections for you." Instead, we actually took those pre-generated things based on what we know about you and put it into the actual project experience itself. (00:58:15): So it tried to get at some of the principles of what a wizard can do well without avoiding the wizard principle, without creating actual wizard. So that's been some of the, how do we work together to get the intent of what the growth ideas but in a way that's consistent with the way we want to build in core?
turns.zh: Onboarding 轮播。某种基本让人不真用产品就 setup 的方式。所以我们总有点 dance around、我们有非常具体的「无 wizard」原则，但我觉得有时张力是 wizard 在某些情况下能 serve 目的，但我们避免做那个。但我们总工作去试图把 wizard 做得好的原则——它把产品简化成让人有更低门槛——带进实际体验本身。所以那实验的例子我提过——给在线商店编辑器预填 sections——你本可以用 wizardy 方式「输几样，我们给你生成这些 sections」。而是我们其实拿那些基于我们对你了解的预生成东西、放进实际项目体验本身。所以它试图拿到 wizard 能做得好的某些原则、而不违反 wizard 原则、不造实际 wizard。所以那是我们怎么一起工作拿到增长想法的 intent、但以跟核心想建的方式一致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And I get why that you think about this a lot because you talked about one of the biggest levers is onboarding and helping more people get activated, and so I could see why you spent a lot of time thinking about how do we help more people succeed there.
turns.zh: 明白了。我懂你为啥想很多这个，因为你提过最大杠杆之一是 onboarding、帮更多人激活，所以我能看为啥你花很多时间想怎么帮更多人在那成功。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to ask your insight on this idea that people might be listening to this and feeling like, "Oh, we need to build a team that just builds great product and is not constrained by metrics and driving growth." Short-term thinking, long-term thinking, 100 years. This is inspiring I think to a lot of companies because the sounds great. (00:59:08): What do you think it takes to make something like that work? Because in a bad case, this team just sits around and builds whatever they want, and the rest of the company's like, "God damn, this sucks. I have to show success in metrics and moving a metric in this team, over there just build beautiful things." Is it like you need a founder like Tobi, that prioritizes this and values it and has a very good taste and intuition? What do you think are important elements of something like that, of this approach working at a company based on what you've seen?
turns.zh: 我想问你对这想法的洞察——可能有人听这觉得「哦我们需要建个不被指标约束、驱动增长的团队。短期想、长期想、100 年」。这 inspiring 我想对很多公司因为听起来超棒。你觉得让那样 work 需要啥？因为在坏 case，这团队就坐那建他们想要的，公司其他人「天，这 sucks。我得在指标上显示成功、move 指标，那团队就在那建漂亮东西」。是需要像 Tobi 的创始人、优先这个、重视它、有非常好的品味和直觉？你觉得那种方式在公司 work 的重要元素是啥，基于你看到的？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, I think it needs to have a very opinionated founder set of people who are driving what good looks like. And I think Shopify a few years ago and before maybe sometimes drifted into the mode of, "We are just going to build stuff and each kind of team is just going to build stuff not really accountable for it," and that is a very, very bad state to end up. So I think you either have to use, my sense is metrics as accountability, which is the most common kind of way to drive accountability and focus. Or extremely strong founder or set of folks who have extremely strong opinions on what good is and what taste is. If you have one of those two, you can make it work, but the worst case is let's just go build a bunch of cool stuff in kind of a haphazard way. That I don't think would work.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得它需要有非常 opinionated 的创始人组人在驱动「好是啥样」。而我觉得 Shopify 几年前和之前有时 drift 进「我们就建东西、每个团队就建东西、不真负责」的模式，那是会 end up 非常糟的状态。所以我觉得你要么用——我的感觉是——指标作为问责，那是最常见的驱动问责和聚焦的方式。要么极强的创始人或一组人对「好是啥、品味是啥」有极强意见。如果你有这两之一，你能让它 work，但最坏情况是「我们就去建一堆酷东西、有点随意」。那我觉得不会 work。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, this is great. So either you need metrics to tell you you're doing the right thing or really correct and good taste in your founder.
turns.zh: 对，这超好。所以要么你需要指标告诉你做对了，要么你创始人真对、好品味。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. I think that's a really good way of... And I imagine every founder is going to think, "Oh, that's me. I have this, I can do this." I think it's rare in real life. It's rare that you're like a Tobi, or Brian Chesky, or Elon.
turns.zh: 酷。我觉得那是真好方式……我猜每个创始人会想「哦那是我。我有这个，我能做」。我觉得真实里罕见。你像 Tobi、Brian Chesky、Elon 那样罕见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's hard to internalize that, but I think that's the reality. So most people will be more successful building things that are driving metrics they can track in an experiment.
turns.zh: 对。那难 internalize，但我觉得那是现实。所以大多数人会更成功建驱动他们能在实验里追的指标的东西。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. This is very fascinating. I'm so happy we're spending so much time on this. Okay, there's a few other random things I'm going to touch on. One is sales. So historically, Shopify has been very product-like growth, very organic. Go check it out, sign up, shop a store, start a store, grow. And you guys have layered on sales. In a sales motion that's an increasing part of your business. What have you learned about your team, the growth team working with sales and making that a successful relationship?
turns.zh: 超棒。这非常迷人。我超高兴我们花这么多时间在这。好，有几个其他随机事我要碰。一是销售。历史上 Shopify 非常产品式增长、非常有机。去看看、注册、逛店、开店、成长。而你们叠了销售——一个销售 motion 成你们业务增加的部分。你从你的团队、增长团队跟销售工作、让那成成功关系，学到了啥？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, no, it has been great over the last couple of years as built out, the sales order has added a whole new kind of motion to Shopify. As Shopify's product got better, it can serve the biggest companies in the world. It's like the natural evolution. Well what are you going to do that for people to grow up on Shopify and to be the biggest companies, but we're also going to take folks another platform, bring them over. (01:01:57): For growth in sales, I think the biggest learning from the the R&D side at least has been the scale is very different with sales, and so it's really hard to use as much quantitative data to make growth, to make some of those decisions. (01:02:18): And so a lot of it has been building much more qualitative insights working with merchant success, sales about the challenges they're facing and onboarding a large customer. So how do we build import tools that work for them? How do we make sure they have the right guidance in the product for a very different set of use cases? So a lot of it has just been very much empathy building with sales about what that merchant journey looks like, and quite frankly challenging ourselves to think differently. It's been one thing. (01:02:49): And then second, we kind of built two very distinct funnels for a little bit. There's a sales funnel. You come in, you contact us, that's it. There's no mention of self-service, there's no this. There's just drive MQLs, boom. Then there's the self-service thing. There's no mention of sales anywhere. (01:03:05): So one of the last thing the year, last year we've been really doing is how do we create these hyper journeys where there is... We shouldn't force the merchant to choose, do you want to talk to sales? You want to do self-service? Should give them the options, whatever path that they want to go on. (01:03:19): And so a lot of that has been building into the self-service journey over to sales and then from sales into self-service. That's broken a lot of metrics in the business. That's broken a lot of ways people have thought about their jobs, and so there's been a lot of cultural resetting and just getting smarter from a metric standpoint about, how do we measure this thing of hybrid journey? They came in via self-service, they went over to sales. How do we value each of those components in the process? And transparently, that's something we're still getting better at, but it's really important to get there.
turns.zh: 对，不，过去几年建起来超棒，销售组织给 Shopify 加了全新 motion。随 Shopify 产品变好，它能服务世界上最大的公司。那是自然进化。嗯，你要为在 Shopify 上长大、变成最大公司的人做啥，但我们也会带别的平台的人过来。对增长和销售，我觉得从 R&D 侧最大的学习是规模非常不同 with 销售，所以很难用那么多定量数据去做增长、做些决定。所以很多是建更多定性洞察、跟商家成功、销售聊他们面对的挑战、和大客户 onboarding。我们怎么建对他们 work 的导入工具？我们怎么确保他们在产品里有对非常不同用例的对的引导？所以很多只是跟销售建同理心关于那商家旅程长啥样、并坦白挑战我们自己不同想。那是一件事。然后二，我们 kind of 建了两个非常不同的漏斗一阵子。有销售漏斗。你进来、联系我们，就那样。没提自助、没这个。就 drive MQL、boom。然后有自助东西。哪都没提销售。所以我们去年最后做的一件事是怎么建这些 hyper 旅程——不该强迫商家选「你想跟销售聊？你想自助？」该给他们选项、无论他们想走的路径。所以很多是建从自助旅程到销售、然后从销售到自助。那 broke 很多 t 里的指标——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of something that broke that would be illustrative of what you're describing?
turns.zh: 有例子某东西 broke、能说明你描述的？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah. So I think that breaks is drive someone from an ad over to self-service. We typically look at only the self-service LTV of that person. But what happens if they come in, they sign up via self-service and then they go talk to sales? They get changed to a sales driven merchant, which means that that value of that merchant, which is usually actually quite large, does not get associated back to that ad campaign. Oh, guess what that means? That means you would probably reduce investment on that ad campaign because you weren't valuing that. Our system had two different models for calculating LTV. Sales driven one, and a self-service one. Uh oh, we're going to make suboptimal investment decisions now by kind of moving things around even though it's the right thing to do. (01:04:55): So a lot of it's in rebuilding all instrumentation, how we do LTV modeling, how we do attribution, how we do incrementality testing across each of those different types of outcomes, because it was not an intuitive thing for us originally because we had built all of these systems with a much more siloed view.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得 broke 的是 drive 人从广告到自助。我们通常只看那人的自助 LTV。但如果他们进来、自助注册、然后去跟销售聊？他们被改成销售驱动商家，意思是那商家的价值——通常其实相当大——不被 associate 回那广告 campaign。哦猜咋着？那意思是你大概会减那广告 campaign 的投资因为你不 valuation 那个。我们的系统有两个不同的 LTV 计算模型。销售驱动一个、自助一个。 Uh oh，我们现在会因移动东西 around 做次优投资决定——即便那是对的做的事。所以很多是重建所有 instrumentation、我们怎么做 LTV 建模、怎么做归因、怎么做跨每种不同结果的增量测试，因为那对我们原不直觉——我们建所有系统时用更 siloed 视图。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, basically attribution gets a lot more complicated. Are you going in a multi-touch attribution direction or is there something even more clever?
turns.zh: 对，基本归因变复杂多。你们走多触点归因方向，还是有更聪明的？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: My rant is I am... Multi-touch attribution as its place. I think ideally what we want to get through is what we really care about is incrementality. So incrementality is kind of the gold standards, for people who are less like attribution measure is, how do you assign value to a given touch point, right? Click, a view, etc. But it doesn't tell you causally what drove something. That's where incrementality tells you. Incrementality test is basically don't show ads on meta for certain number of people. Show it to the other set, see what the lift is and the outcome. (01:06:04): A lot of what we're doing is trying to get a lot, is continuing to get even more sophisticated in incrementality measurement for not just self-serve outcomes, but for self-service outcomes that then drive to sales for sales specific outcomes. And as soon as we have that kind of incrementality at the channel level, we can get a lot more sophisticated in terms of our bidding, budgeting, and all of that. But that's really the key thing we want to get to.
turns.zh: 我的 rant 是我是……多触点归因有它的位置。我觉得理想我们想达到的是我们真 care 的是增量 (incrementality)。所以增量是金标准——对不那么像归因测量的人，归因测量是「你怎么 assign 价值给给定触点」，点击、浏览等。但它不因果告诉你啥驱动了啥。那是增量告诉你的。增量测试基本是「别在某些人上 show 广告在 meta、给另一组 show、看 lift 和结果」。我们很多在做的是试图拿到更多 sophistication 在增量测量——不只自助结果，而是自助结果然后 drive 到销售、针对销售的特定结果。一旦我们在渠道级有那种增量，我们能在竞价、预算等上更聪明。但那真是我们想达到的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's certain topics that alone can be their own podcast conversation to just dive deep into this stuff. But I'm going to stop myself and I'll go further down that track. Let me touch on a couple more things before I let you go. (01:06:46): One is marketing. So we talked about sales, marketing. You guys don't have a CMO, there's no Shopify CMO. Instead you embed marketing leads within the org. For folks that are trying to grapple with that, should we hire CMO? Should we do something else? What have you learned about maybe the benefits and also maybe some downsides of approaching it the way you guys have approached it?
turns.zh: 有某些话题单独能成自己的播客对话深挖这东西。但我停自己、不 deeper 那条路。让我在放你走前碰几个更多事。一是营销。我们聊了销售、营销。你们没有 CMO，没有 Shopify CMO。而是你们把营销 lead embed 在组织里。对试图 grasp 那个的人，我们该雇 CMO 吗？该做别的吗？你学到啥关于你们 approach 的好处、也许一些 downside？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: The benefit is, so there's growth marketing who sits in growth, there's revenue marketing who sits over closer to sales. There's a brand team under Harley who does amazing work. Our president. There's marketing embedded in core and PMM, sit with the product managers there. There's shop marketing on a consumer side. So marketing is truly everywhere in the org. (01:07:28): And I think the benefit of it is it's closest to the primary goal that those marketers are trying to do. They sit with growth so we can focus on that self-service motion. Harley is an amazing communicator, so brand sits with him so he can have a lot of influence over that. And so I think it sits with the people its most relevant outcomes are driving, which is great. It allows us move faster with less kind of coordination. (01:07:58): I think it only works because Tobi and Harley has such amazing intuition on what the brand is, needs to be, and all of that. Some of what the CMO does of kind of creating the cohesive story of Shopify it held in their heads and they have the pen on that. (01:08:19): And so that allows then, that piece of that CMO's job to not be as important at Shopify. But the other pieces are obviously critical, but they can be now closer to the action and where they're going to drive the most impact. The downside is things are sometimes very messy. So that's...
turns.zh: 好处是：有增长营销坐在增长里、有营收营销坐在更靠近销售、有 Harley 下的品牌团队做惊人工作（我们的总裁）。有营销 embed 在核心、PMM 跟那的产品经理坐。有消费者侧的 shop 营销。所以营销真无处不在。我觉得好处是它 closest 到那些营销人想做的主要目标。他们跟增长坐所以我们聚焦自助 motion。Harley 是惊人沟通者，所以品牌跟他坐让他有很大影响。所以我觉得它坐在这对它的相关结果 drive 的人那，超棒。它让我们更快 move、更少协调。我觉得它只 work 因为 Tobi 和 Harley 对品牌该是啥有如此惊人直觉。CMO 做的某些——建 Shopify 的 cohesive 故事——在他们脑子里、他们有那 pen。所以那让 CMO 工作的那块在 Shopify 不那重要。但其他块 obviously critical，但他们现在更近行动、他们 drive 最多影响的地方。Downside 是事情有时非常 messy。所以那是……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's another example where the founder, their background and interest in skills can impact significantly the way the work is structured and who you hire and don't hire. Okay, one last question. Totally different topic, discounting. So you worked at Udemy for a long time. And from what I understand, discounting was one of the key reasons Udemy succeeded and one of the big differentiators. I'm curious what you learned about discounting, the power of discounting as a growth lever.
turns.zh: 那是另一个例子——创始人他们的背景、兴趣和技能能显著影响工作怎么结构、你雇不雇谁。好，最后一个问题。完全不同话题，折扣 (discounting)。你在 Udemy 工作了很久。据我所知，折扣是 Udemy 成功的关键原因之一、和大差异化之一。我好奇你学到啥关于折扣、折扣作为增长杠杆的力量。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Yeah, so Udemy is a very an online marketplace for online courses. So come on course. And I think what was happening in I started, and we were there 2012-ish was people were like, "What is this online course thing? I don't really understand what it is. I don't understand what the value is and what I'm willing to pay." (01:09:30): And so what discounting has a really powerful effect on is it can signal value with a high list price, but then bring something down to an affordable price. And that may seem like of course that's obvious, but in online courses what was important is the list price would be high at 100 bucks. So it's associated with a college course. But what people really value this thing as was a book. (01:09:54): And so you could signal very high, signal quality through price, which was very murky at that point in online learning. Signal value through price. Discount it to 10 bucks, or that was a typical Udemy deal. And then so 99% off, 90% off. We might see fire sales, but it changed the value in willingness to pay and then it tapped into the fact that, and still is education is very aspirational. (01:10:23): And so what a lot of people missed in education is yes, we want people to actually take the course, but that's actually in many cases not the job to be done. That there's an emotional job that's even more important, which is I'm feeling like I'm making progress in my educational journey, and just the act of purchasing a course or the act of buying a book is progress. (01:10:47): And so if you can make it very enticing, very high value thing, cheap, urgency, you can let people make that emotional journey by the act of purchasing, which then allowed us to actually have very good retention. Because you could keep coming back to that emotional job over and over again, which just counting with urgency allowed us to do.
turns.zh: 对，Udemy 是非常在线的在线课程市场。我来时——我们那大概 2012——人们在「这在线课程是啥？我不太懂它是啥、不懂价值和我愿付啥」。折扣有超强效果的是：它能用高标价 signal 价值、然后带到一个付得起的价。那可能看起来 obvious，但在在线课程重要的是标价会高到 100 块——关联大学课程。但人们真 value 这东西像本书。所以你能通过价格 signal 很高、signal 质量——那会在在线学习当时很 murky。通过价格 signal 价值。discount 到 10 块，或那是典型 Udemy deal。然后 99% off、90% off。我们可能看到 fire sales，但它改了支付意愿的价值、然后它 tap 进事实——教育至今非常有抱负。很多人漏的是：是的我们要人真上课，但那其实在很多 case 不是 job to be done。有个甚至更重要的情感 job——「我感觉我在教育旅程中在进步」，而光是买课的行为、买书的行为就是进步。所以如果你能让它极诱人、极高价值东西、便宜、紧迫，你能让人通过购买行为做那情感旅程，那让我们能有非常好留存。因为你能一遍遍回到那情感 job，而用紧迫计数让我们能做。

turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，你最推荐给别人的两三本书？

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: So one, I love to go back to marketers who wrote in the 1920s. And so one that I love is Scientific Advertising by Claude Hopkins. So it's basically one of the first direct marketers that came out and he innovated on some of the concepts of copywriting and just how you sell a product around can't make this product, can't sell the product, can you tell the product will help the customer achieve their goals? And so it's really fun. I find it really fun to go back in time, because there's a lot of really good first principles thinking that I think we've actually lost in more modern stuff where it's like personalization band, it's optimization, all this stuff. Where it's like how do you actually write and sell things really effectively? Scientific Advertising, it's a great book.
turns.zh: 一，我爱回去看 1920 年代写的市场人。我爱的一个是 Claude Hopkins 的《Scientific Advertising》（科学广告）。他基本是最早的直复营销人之一，他创新了一些文案概念、就你怎么卖产品——不能造这产品、不能卖这产品，你能告诉这产品会帮客户达到目标吗？所以真好玩。我觉得回过去时间真好玩，因为有很多真好的第一性原理思考——我觉得我们在更现代的东西里其实丢了，像个性化 band、优化、所有这堆。而「你怎么真有效写和卖东西？」《Scientific Advertising》是好書。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's just like the name alone, it sounds really cool. Especially for someone in your shoes that feels like the perfect book for your role. And I think there's so much wisdom in just the thing someone figured out many years ago about what convinces people to buy something is still true and people overcomplicate it. Just going back to the original is often really useful.
turns.zh: 光名字就听起来超酷。尤其对你这种角色的人，那像为你角色完美的书。而且我觉得很多智慧就在「某人多年前搞清啥说服人买东西仍真、人们把它 overcomplicate」这一点。回原典常真有用。

turns.speaker: Archie Abrams
turns.en: Totally. And The Perfect Mile about the chase for sub four minute mile by Roger Bannister and a few other folks is just a wonderful... As a runner, it's a really fun book to read about perseverance, how these folks really, they all competed to get to that really amazing goal of under four minutes in a mile.
turns.zh: 完全。还有《The Perfect Mile》——关于 Roger Bannister 等几人追 sub 四分钟 mile——就美妙……作为跑者，读关于坚持、这些人怎么真全竞争到那超棒目标（四分钟一英里）超好玩。

turns.en: Yeah.

turns.zh: 哦天。好多看，我做过一次、我想「我有好多集要看」，但 incredible。好。有趣你说《Sopranos》。我感觉最近几个人告诉我他们在重看整部《Sopranos》。像最近某种 trend。

turns.zh: Suno 是 Insane。我想是 Suno.ai，人们想看。它也是超好玩的 party trick——当场写首关于你想的事的歌。超棒。还有两个问题。你有常回到的、觉得有用的人生格言，工作生活里？

But acknowledge it might change and we'll deal with it then. But if the combination of we have a plan, stay focused on that, with also the acknowledgement that you need to be flexible, and try to combine those two sometimes contradictory things of focus plan with we got to be able to react in an effective way.
turns.zh: 对，我常回到「计划就是计划直到它不是」(the plan is the plan until it's not)。基本我们有计划。它是计划、是我们最好的、让我们 commit 它。但承认它可能变、我们那时 deal with 它。但是「我们有计划、聚焦那」加「承认你得灵活」的组合，试着 combine 这两个有时矛盾的东西——聚焦计划，加我们得能有效反应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me of strong opinions loosely held as a concept.

turns.en: Totally.

turns.zh: 对。我爸很多是个父亲，他是科技创业者。我觉得我超 appreciate 他领导风格的一件事是同理心、好奇、和他在一切里展现的善良。我希望在他的一些故事里——无论谁，他都好奇、爱 engage 和学。我希望那是我想 take inspiration 的——对每个人善良、从你身边每个人学。所以是我常想的。

turns.zh: 那超共鸣。他听起来像奇妙的人，你也是。Archie，这超棒。我们碰了这么多。cover 了这么多。我觉得我们能再聊好多小时。也许你学到更多东西时我们做第二轮。最后两个问题。人们想联系你在线、或 follow 你在上搞啥，以及听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.en: So not super on social media. But on LinkedIn, check me out, send me a message. turns.en: Yes. Yes.
